newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SINGAPORE SHARES HIT AGAIN BY DUAL LISTINGS FEARS.
newsitem.headline: SINGAPORE SHARES HIT AGAIN BY DUAL LISTINGS FEARS.

text.p: Trading in Singapore blue chips was volatitle on Thursday as fund managers continued be concerned over the fate of the dual listing system of local and foreign share tranches.

An overnight announcement by government-owned Singapore Technologies that it had scrapped the foreign and local share tranches of its four units listed on the Stock Exchange of Singapore re-ignited fears over the fate of dual listings.

Shares of ST Aerospace, ST Automotive and ST Electronic & Engineering jumped sharply in early trade to new year highs. ST Shipbuilding & Engineering rose over 13 percent but stopped short of its year high of Singapore $1.97.

But the foreign share tranches of Singapore's four major banks dived. Overseas Union Bank, United Overseas Bank and OCBC Bank plunged to new year lows in heavy dealings. DBS Bank foreign shares suffered the least damage but still shed 50 cents or 3.5 percent to S$16.90.
Meanwhile, the respective local bank tranches rallied, rising by between 3.4 percent to 7.7 percent.

Dealers and analysts said most fund managers were not really comforted by a Monetary Authority of Singapore statement that there would be no changes in the 40 percent limit on foreign shareholdings for banks.
Statements from Singapore Airlines (SIA) and Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) that they had no plans to change their dual listings were also ignored as funds dumped foreign tranches.

"The authorities have been very clear and the companies have said they will not make any changes. But funds just don't believe them. It is a case of investors trying not to take risks and they are expecting the worse," said Lim Jit Soon, head of research at UBS Securities.

"These companies will not make any changs right now as they don't want to hurt their foreign shareholders too much. But the truth is that if the premiums between local and foreign shares narrow sharply, most will probably scrap their dual listings," a fund manager with a Singapore corporation said.
Singapore Technologies said one of the reasons for scrapping the system was because of "narrowing price differentials".
Dual listings were originally introduced to protect companies considered to be strategically important to Singapore.
Dealers and analsyts said the system has evolved to be quite inefficient and there were other ways of to retain control these key companies, like having special management shares.
While prices of local share tranches have stagnated for the past few years because of poor liquidity, foreign tranches have rallied with foreign funds pouring into the region.
The premium between the tranches can be huge, with SPH local trading at S$13.40, or about half the price of its foreign share which was at S$25.10 in late afternoon on Thursday.
"Everybody concerned has realised it is not necessarily desirable to either the companies or their shareholders," said a dealer. "It is a bit clumsy."
Hugh Young, managing director of Aberdeen Asset Management, which runs one of the few Singapore-only funds, agreed.
"Longer term, the world is not going the way of local and foreign share tranches. It is becoming deregulated," he said.

When that would happen in Singapore is still a big question. But in the meantime, analysts say local shares offer great value as most are priced attractively and trading below their net tangible asset value.
"I still think local shares -- SIA, SPH, the four big banks -- are cheap, possibly 20-30 percent cheap," Young said.
